geom.title: Worthing–Brighton: what the globe needs to show a laser 1 m above the sea
geom.mini: Across {{pD}} km of sea, a laser 1 m above the water is hidden by {{pHid}} m from a camera 1 m up, for straight light. It is seen if the air bends light with k = {{pK}}: air warming by {{pG2}} °C over its first 2 m.
geom.text: In February 2019 a group fired lasers between Worthing Pier and Brighton's West Pier, {{pD}} km apart, lasers and cameras about 1 m above the water, and saw them [1]. Their slides compute the globe correctly: the sea bulges {{pBulge}} m between the piers, and for straight light the laser is {{pHid}} m below the camera's horizon ({{pHidStd}} m with the usual k = 0.13). What they leave out is how little air it takes to change that. The camera sees the laser once the effective radius R/(1 − k) passes d²/2(√h_s + √h_c)², a uniform k of {{pK}}: at that evening's pressure, air warming with height by {{pG2}} °C between the water and 2 m.
geom.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the laser seen again and again from 1 m at 15 km while thermometers good to 0.05 °C show no warming with height. Would favour the globe: the same beam hidden under the same thermometers.
therm.title: Their thermometers measured the air that shows the laser
therm.mini: The globe needs the air to warm by {{pG2}} °C over 2 m. At Worthing the operators' two thermometers read {{pWdT}} °C. At Brighton they read nothing they could resolve: their ±0.25 °C allows anything from {{pBlo}} to {{pBhi}} °C per metre.
therm.text: The refraction coefficient follows the vertical temperature gradient, k = 503·P/T²·(0.0342 + dT/dh) [2]: each 0.1 °C per metre of warming adds 0.66 to k on that evening. The operators read the air at several heights at both ends with two thermometers good to ±0.25 °C, read to the half degree [1]. At Worthing both show the air warming by {{pWdT}} °C over 2 m, {{pRatio}} times what the globe needs for the laser to be seen. At Brighton the readings are flat between the water and {{pBdh}} m, which their precision cannot tell from any gradient between {{pBlo}} and {{pBhi}} °C per metre, the needed one included. Their thermometers could not rule out the air that decides the test, and at one end they measured it.
therm.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the laser seen while thermometers ten times finer show the air not warming with height, at both ends and halfway.
evenings.title: Two evenings, two answers: the laser follows the air
evenings.mini: 2 February 2019: air {{p2T}} °C over a {{p2S}} °C sea, wind {{p2W}} km/h; the laser was not seen. 23 February: air {{p23T}} °C, sea {{p23S}} °C, light wind; it was seen. The operators blamed refraction for the first and denied it for the second.
evenings.text: The same test was tried twice [1]. On 2 February ERA5 puts the air 2 m above the sea at {{p2T}} °C over a sea at {{p2S}} °C (OISST), with a {{p2W}} km/h wind off the land [2][3]: cold air over warmer water bends low rays upward, and the laser vanishes on a globe and on a plane alike. On 23 February the air offshore was as warm as the sea under a light wind, the water at the beaches no warmer than the air: the warm-over-cold layer that lets a low beam follow the sea's curve. The operators put the first evening's failure down to a refraction zone above the sea, and concluded from the second that no refraction occurred.
evenings.verdict: A verdict fixed in advance must count both evenings the same way. Would favour the flat plane: the laser seen on both, whatever the air.
anim.title: Worthing–Brighton 2019, ray by ray: the air decides, not the shape
anim.mini: A laser 1 m above the sea, a camera 1 m up {{pD}} km away, traced on a globe and a plane in the same air. 2 February, cold air: hidden on both, as it was. 23 February, the air measured at Worthing: seen on the globe directly, on the plane by reflection.
anim.text: The operators of the Worthing–Brighton test saw a laser 1 m above the sea from 1 m up, {{pD}} km away, on 23 February 2019, and could not see it on 2 February [1]. Traced ray by ray, 81 rays of a 1 mrad beam, through each evening's air: on 2 February, air {{p2T}} °C over a {{p2S}} °C sea (ERA5, OISST) [2][3], the beam is thrown upward and misses the camera on the globe and on the plane alike. On 23 February, in the air their thermometers measured at Worthing, warming by {{pWdT}} °C over 2 m, the globe shows the beam directly and the plane only by reflection off calm water. In the air measured at Brighton, flat within their precision, the globe hides it. The globe needs only +{{pG2}} °C over 2 m, less than their thermometers could resolve.
anim.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the laser seen from 1 m at 15 km, again and again, while thermometers ten times finer show no warming with height. Would favour the globe: the same beam hidden under those thermometers.
